pr_title: Refactor XXX_do_all_provided() to behave like XXX_fetch()
pr_body:
This is refactored to use inner_xxx_fetch() without any given
name, which is just there to ensure all decoder implementations are
made into methods, and then use ossl_method_store_do_all() to list
them all.

This also adds the internal xxx_do_all_prefetched(), which
can be used if pre-fetching needs to be done separately from listing
all the decoder implementations, or if listing may happen multiple
times.

Fixes #15538
Fixes #14837

...

Each sample counts as 0.01 seconds.

...

That's 1000 times fewer calls, i.e. 1000 times less allocations of the same methods!

> ...and yet, where all the providers allow caching, and no providers have been activated or deactivated they should be really fast after the first call. Can we optimise this somehow?

They are substantially faster after the first fetch (up until the store is dropped)...  I did a quick program to demonstrate that to myself, and got the first fetch at 0.001544 s, while the following ones were at about 0.000022 s.  So I take it that the argument is that it's still not fast enough, rather than what I thought I heard earlier, that there's currently no check of this sort at all.

~I'm quite confident that this can be optimized.  As a matter of fact, since `ossl_algorithm_do_all()` is now only used in one place, in `ossl_method_construct()`, we could merge `crypto/core_fetch.c` with `crypto/core_algorithm.c` and do some pretty heavy refactoring to reduce the layering that is now no longer needed.~
~(side note: I propose that the code from `crypto/core_fetch.c` gets moved to `crypto/core_algorithm.c` and that `crypto/core_fetch.c` gets dropped).~

~The question is if that sort of optimization is:~
1.  ~to be done in this PR or another~
2.  ~must be done for beta1~

UPDATE:

My confidence went away quite quickly...  I was naïvely thinking that we could make the pre-condition, i.e. the check if we have already loaded the algos with the given operation identity, earlier in `ossl_construct_method()` and thereby avoid this:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/0051746e03c65f5970d8ca424579d50f58a877e0/crypto/core_fetch.c#L116

Alas, that would destroy any chances of loading any algorithm with `no_store` set, so that optimization would be a functional downgrade.  I'm not sure how to deal with that for the moment...  that will require a bit more though.

Demonstration program:

``` C
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <sys/times.h>
#include <openssl/decoder.h>

#ifndef LOOPS
#    define LOOPS 10
#endif
#ifndef LOOP_ITERATIONS
#    define LOOP_ITERATIONS 1000
#endif

int main()
{
    struct tms tms1, tms2, tms3;
    clock_t c1, c2, c3;
    int i, j;

    c1 = clock();
    times(&tms1);
    (void)OSSL_DECODER_fetch(NULL, NULL, NULL);
    c2 = clock();
    times(&tms2);
    (void)OSSL_DECODER_fetch(NULL, NULL, NULL);
    c3 = clock();
    times(&tms3);

    printf("First fetch:\n"
           "  real time: %f s\n"
           "  user time: %f s\n"
           "  sys  time: %f s\n",
           (double)(c2 - c1) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
           (double)(tms2.tms_utime - tms1.tms_utime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
           (double)(tms2.tms_stime - tms1.tms_stime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    printf("Second fetch:\n"
           "  real time: %f s\n"
           "  user time: %f s\n"
           "  sys  time: %f s\n",
           (double)(c3 - c2) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
           (double)(tms3.tms_utime - tms2.tms_utime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
           (double)(tms3.tms_stime - tms2.tms_stime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);

    for (i = 0; i++ < LOOPS;) {
        struct tms ltms1, ltms2;
        clock_t lc1, lc2;

        lc1 = clock();
        times(&ltms1);
        for (j = LOOP_ITERATIONS; j-- > 0;)
            (void)OSSL_DECODER_fetch(NULL, NULL, NULL);
        lc2 = clock();
        times(&ltms2);

        printf("%d fetches, iteration %d:\n"
               "  real time: %f s (%f s per fetch)\n"
               "  user time: %f s (%f s per fetch)\n"
               "  sys  time: %f s (%f s per fetch)\n",
               LOOP_ITERATIONS, i,
               (double)(lc2 - lc1) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
               (double)(lc2 - lc1) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC / 1000,
               (double)(ltms2.tms_utime - ltms1.tms_utime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
               (double)(ltms2.tms_utime - ltms1.tms_utime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC / LOOP_ITERATIONS,
               (double)(ltms2.tms_stime - ltms1.tms_stime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC,
               (double)(ltms2.tms_stime - ltms1.tms_stime) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC / LOOP_ITERATIONS);
    }
}
```

issue_context.title: XXX_do_all_provided() recreates every method, every time it's called.
issue_context.body:
At the time these functions were created, their use were limited to `openssl list`.
However, with encoders and decoders, their use became more extensive...  and costly, because they don't "fetch" in a way that allows storing away the fetched methods for later use.

For more optimum use, these need to be modified to internally behave closer to the usual fetches.

This should not affect public APIs
comments: Fixing this should fix #14837 as well.

To avoid sign extension when downshifting.
Shouldn't matter that much, I would say that it would be a challenge to produce 2^23 names too :wink:
Shifting an unsigned value right is a logical shift.

Yeah, but it's passed to `ossl_method_store_cache_set()`, which takes it as an `int`, which in turn affects `filter_on_operation_id()` further down.

It's possible that we should change `ossl_method_store_cache_set()`, but that may explode, so I'd rather have that done in a different PR.

My thought he was why bother packing this at all.

I didn't think it important enough to comment on -- 8,000,000+ names ought to be sufficient for a while.

> My thought he was why bother packing this at all.

Because this needs to be passed as the "nid" (which isn't the same as the NIDs) to `ossl_method_store_cache_set()`, and this method ID is specific to EVP fetch functions.  The OSSL_DECODER, OSSL_ENCODER and OSSL_STORE_LOADER fetching is simple, there is no operation ID to account for, since they use entirely separate method stores.
This explanation should be a comment in the code...
